lines.text: In nineteen seventy-seven, something in deep space broke through the static for seventy-two seconds. This video lasts exactly that long.
August fifteenth. Ohio State's Big Ear telescope listens to the sky, and a computer prints what it hears.
Most of the page is noise. Then, six characters. Six. E. Q. U. J. Five.
Every letter means louder. U means thirty times louder than the background.
Days later, volunteer Jerry Ehman circled it in red, and wrote one word.
Big Ear couldn't move. Earth's spin swept the sky past it, so anything out in space would rise and fall over seventy-two seconds. This did.
It sat near fourteen twenty megahertz, the natural frequency of hydrogen.
Big Ear had two receivers. It should have heard the signal twice. It heard it once. Decades of searching since. Nothing.
In twenty twenty-four, researchers proposed a natural cause. A hydrogen cloud, briefly lit by a burst from a magnetar. Maybe.
But for seventy-two seconds, the sky got loud. And we only heard it once.
